title: Plan Your DSA Preparation in Eight Weeks
audience: Candidates who can implement simple programs and want a structured progression from foundational patterns to mixed interview problems, with enough review to retain and transfer the learning.
summary: Study data structures through the operations they support and algorithms through the invariants that make them correct. Use topic-focused practice to learn, then mixed unseen problems to test recognition. A complete preparation loop includes clarification, implementation, testing, complexity, and revision.
outcomes: Choose an approach from constraints rather than a visible topic label.
Explain the invariant and complexity of common interview patterns.
Implement and test solutions without relying on memorized templates.
Use a spaced error log and mixed mocks to measure transfer.
foundations: Constraints select techniques

Input size, ordering, value range, mutation rules, and output requirements change the solution. A quadratic method may be acceptable for small input; a sliding window may fail when negative values break monotonicity. Read the contract before naming a pattern.
Data structures encode operations

Maps support keyed lookup, heaps expose an extreme, queues process arrival order, and ordered structures support range reasoning. Compare the operations required by the problem with the actual cost and memory of the chosen structure.
Proof and testing complement each other

An invariant explains all valid executions; tests expose mistakes in the implementation or assumptions. Do both. A solution that passes a few examples can still be wrong, while a correct idea can be implemented with an off-by-one defect.
studyRule: Use three focused problem sessions, one review session, and one mixed mock each week. Re-solve failures from a blank editor after a delay. Record the missed clue and invariant, not a copied solution paragraph or only a completion checkbox.
plan: Weeks 1-2
Linear structures and search

Cover arrays, maps, sets, pointers, windows, stacks, and binary search. Trace indexes and counts explicitly. Practice both a simple baseline and one optimization, explaining what repeated work was removed.
Independent solutions with tests for minimal input, duplicates, boundaries, and invalid assumptions.
Weeks 3-4
Trees, heaps, and graphs
Study recursion, iterative traversal, BFS, DFS, priority queues, connected components, and topological order. Distinguish node identity from value and directed cycles from undirected parent edges.
A traversal notebook with visited timing, queue/stack state, and time complexity in vertices and edges.
Weeks 5-6
State and choice

Practice backtracking, greedy arguments, intervals, and dynamic programming. Define states before recurrences and justify greedy choices with an exchange or dominance argument. Compare memoization with bottom-up evaluation.
Several solved variants that demonstrate why a method applies, plus a counterexample where it does not.
Weeks 7-8
Mixed execution

Use unseen mixed sets and realistic time limits. Preserve time for tests and complexity. Add role-relevant harder problems only after medium-level correctness is stable. Review recurring failures and reduce new material near the interview.
A recent mock scorecard and a short revision list tied to observed weaknesses rather than a target problem count.

lab.title: Choose the pattern from a changed constraint
lab.scenario: You are asked for a shortest contiguous subarray with sum at least a target. In one version every value is positive; in another values may be negative. The word 'subarray' alone does not determine the algorithm.
steps: For positive values, adding to the right cannot decrease the sum and removing from the left cannot increase it. This supports expanding until valid and shrinking while preserving validity to minimize length.

Introduce a negative value and construct a case where removing an element increases the sum or extending lowers it. Explain exactly which monotone argument fails; do not reuse the same window mechanically.

Study an appropriate prefix-sum and monotonic-deque method for the general version, or state a correct slower baseline first. Compare contracts, complexity, and edge cases before implementing the advanced variant.
lab.result: The learning artifact is the distinction between the two contracts and their proofs. Recognizing why an approach stops applying is as valuable as remembering when it works.
checks: Can you state the monotonic property in the positive-input version?
Does your counterexample actually break the reused window rule?
Are empty results and impossible targets handled according to the problem?
lab.extension: Change 'shortest' to 'number of exact-sum subarrays.' Explain why prefix-frequency counts become useful and why storing only one prior prefix index would lose valid answers.

qa: Should I finish one topic completely before moving on?

Build enough understanding to implement and explain the basic pattern, then revisit it in mixed practice. There is no finite point where a topic is completely finished; spaced transfer is more useful than endless near-identical exercises.
How should I use solution explanations?

Attempt the problem, identify the exact blocker, read only enough to learn the missing idea, then implement independently and explain it. Revisit after a delay and test a variation to avoid mistaking recognition for mastery.
When should I practice hard problems?

When they teach a relevant new technique or stretch stable fundamentals. If basic implementation and testing remain unreliable, hard-problem memorization can hide rather than fix the main preparation gap.
pitfalls: Selecting a pattern from the title while ignoring constraints.
Counting copied solutions as independent practice.
Skipping correctness reasoning and tests to maximize volume.
readiness: Mixed unseen problems can be approached without category hints.
Each solution includes a clear invariant and complexity.
Boundary cases are tested before completion is declared.
The error log drives specific re-solves and variations.

title: Arrays, Hashing, and Two-Pointer Reasoning
audience: Learners who know loops and collections and want to understand common linear and near-linear solutions without memorizing a separate trick for every array problem.
summary: Arrays give indexed access and locality; hashing trades memory for keyed lookup; two pointers exploit ordering or a maintained partition. The useful skill is recognizing which information must be retained and which candidate region can be discarded safely.
outcomes: Choose between sorting, hashing, and pointer movement using the input contract.
Handle duplicates, multiplicities, and index-versus-value requirements correctly.
State the invariant behind complement lookup and sorted two-pointer search.
Analyze expected hash-table cost and auxiliary space honestly.
foundations: Values and positions are different

A problem may ask for original indexes, unique values, or all valid pairs. Sorting can destroy original positional information unless it is retained. Duplicates may be legitimate separate positions rather than redundant values to discard.
Hashing stores the missing information

For complement search, retain previously seen values and their indexes. For frequency questions, store counts rather than membership. Expected constant-time operations depend on the implementation and assumptions; do not describe every hash lookup as a worst-case guarantee.
Pointer movement needs a proof

In a sorted sum problem, if the sum is too small, reducing the right value cannot help, so move the left pointer. Without ordering, this elimination argument is invalid. An in-place compaction pointer instead represents the boundary of already processed valid output.
studyRule: For each exercise, write the required output and duplicate policy first. Solve a small baseline, then explain what the map or pointer invariant eliminates. Test repeated values and an answer involving the same numeric value at two different positions.
plan: Days 1-3
Array contracts

Practice traversal, stable compaction, prefix/suffix accumulation, and in-place updates. Distinguish logical length from capacity and check whether input mutation is allowed. Trace read and write positions on paper.
A compaction example that preserves order and never overwrites unread data.
Days 4-6
Maps and counts

Study complement lookup, duplicates, anagrams, and frequency grouping. Decide whether the map stores a count, earliest index, latest index, or a list of positions. Explain memory growth and missing-key behavior.
Several examples where using a set instead of a count or index map would be wrong.
Days 7-10
Sorted pointer methods
Practice pair sums, deduplicated triples, and merging sorted sequences. Justify each pointer movement and where duplicates should be skipped. Preserve original indexes if the output requires them.
A sorted-pair proof and a merge trace that handles equal values and empty inputs.
Days 11-14
Mixed variants
Change one requirement at a time: return counts, preserve order, forbid mutation, or allow repeated results. Compare sorting and hashing under those constraints and run an unseen timed problem.
A decision table connecting contract changes to data-structure and complexity changes.

lab.title: Find a pair without reusing the same element
lab.scenario: Given values [3, 3, 4] and target 6, return two distinct indexes. A value-only set can show that 3 exists, but careless ordering can pair an element with itself.
steps: Scan from left to right and look up target minus current value before inserting the current index. At index zero, the complement is absent, so record value 3 at index zero.

At index one, the complement 3 is already recorded at index zero. Return indexes zero and one. The invariant is that the map contains only earlier positions, so the two indexes are necessarily distinct.

Compare with sorting indexed pairs and using two pointers. That method costs sorting time but can be useful for other output contracts. Explain why simply sorting raw values would lose original indexes.
lab.result: The complement method uses expected O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space, with a clear distinct-index guarantee. It does not require that values themselves be distinct.
checks: Does target 6 with input [3] correctly report no pair?
Are duplicate values handled according to the requested output?
Does the method preserve original indexes when required?
lab.extension: Return the number of all index pairs instead of the first pair. Replace the stored index with a frequency count and explain why each earlier matching occurrence contributes one new pair.

qa: When is sorting better than hashing?

Sorting may support ordered output, range reasoning, duplicate grouping, or lower auxiliary-memory requirements depending on the language. Compare the full contract, including whether mutation and loss of original order are acceptable.
Why does a set fail for some anagram or pair-count questions?

Membership does not preserve multiplicity. Two strings can use the same character set with different counts, and repeated values can create several distinct index pairs. Store the information the output actually depends on.
Can two pointers always make an array problem linear?
No. The method needs a monotone elimination or partition invariant. Without that structure, moving a pointer may discard a valid solution. Name the proof, not just the technique.
pitfalls: Inserting before complement lookup and accidentally reusing an index.
Discarding duplicates that are meaningful to the output.
Claiming worst-case O(1) hash operations without qualification.
readiness: The map value's meaning is explicit.
Every pointer movement has a correctness argument.
Mutation and original-order requirements are respected.
Duplicate and minimal-input cases have been traced.

title: Sliding Windows and Prefix Sums
audience: Candidates who recognize subarray and substring questions but need to distinguish fixed windows, variable windows, and prefix-state methods correctly.
summary: Contiguous-range problems often become efficient when you maintain only the state that changes at the boundaries. Sliding windows use a safe expand/shrink rule; prefix sums turn a range relationship into a relationship between earlier states. The input constraints determine which reasoning applies.
outcomes: Define window validity and update it correctly as boundaries move.
Recognize when negative values or exact-count requirements break a simple window.
Use prefix-frequency maps to count all matching ranges.
Test off-by-one, empty-prefix, and duplicate-prefix cases deliberately.
foundations: Fixed windows update two boundaries

For a window of length k, add the incoming value and remove the outgoing one. Carefully define when the first full window exists. For character problems, compare multiplicities, not only distinct membership.
Variable windows need monotonicity

A window can shrink greedily only when the validity rule supports it. Positive sums and at-most-k distinct counts have useful monotone behavior; arbitrary negative sums do not follow the same rule. State what remains true after every boundary update.
Prefixes encode history

If current prefix sum is S, a subarray of target sum T ends here for every earlier prefix equal to S-T. Initialize the empty prefix once. Store counts when several earlier prefixes can produce distinct ranges.
studyRule: Draw indexes and window state for a short example before coding. Use separate exercises for maximum/minimum length and number of matching ranges; they often need different retained information. Explain why the left boundary never moves backward when that is your invariant.
plan: Sessions 1-3
Fixed-size windows
Practice rolling sums and anagram windows. Validate k and input length, update incoming and outgoing counts, and decide whether the result is a value, index, or list of windows.
A trace showing the first valid window and every subsequent update without recomputing the whole range.
Sessions 4-6
Variable-size windows

Study unique-character windows, replacement budgets, and minimum positive-sum windows. Define the validity predicate and the reason shrinking is safe. Test repeated characters near the current left boundary.
A proof that each index is advanced at most a bounded number of times and no valid candidate is skipped.
Sessions 7-10
Prefix sums and counts

Practice exact subarray sums with zero and negative values. Compare storing counts, earliest positions, and all positions. Initialize the empty prefix and avoid inserting the current prefix too early for the intended contract.
Worked examples with repeated prefix values and a clear count of distinct subarrays.
Sessions 11-14
Mixed decisions

Remove topic labels and solve variants involving circular arrays, bounds, and exact versus at-most constraints. Explain a counterexample for an inappropriate window approach before selecting an alternative.
An unseen mixed problem solved with a justified choice and boundary tests.

lab.title: Count zero-sum subarrays with repeated prefixes
lab.scenario: For values [1, -1, 1, -1] and target zero, count every contiguous range whose sum is zero. Negative values make a simple positive-sum shrinking window unreliable.
steps: Start with prefix frequency {0: 1}, representing the empty prefix. After reading 1, the current sum is 1 and there are no earlier prefixes with that sum; then record frequency 1 for prefix 1.

After -1, the current sum is 0 and one earlier zero prefix contributes one range. Record zero frequency 2. At the next 1, one earlier prefix 1 contributes another range; record frequency 2 for prefix 1.

At the final -1, the current sum is zero and two earlier zero prefixes contribute two more ranges. The total is four. Looking up before recording avoids counting an empty range at the current position.
lab.result: Four zero-sum subarrays are counted in expected O(n) time using prefix frequencies. The map stores multiplicity because distinct earlier boundaries can have the same sum.
checks: Does an all-zero array of length three produce six nonempty zero-sum ranges?
Is the empty prefix initialized exactly once?
Does the implementation distinguish counts from a single remembered index?
lab.extension: Ask for the longest zero-sum range instead. Store the earliest index for each prefix sum and explain why later duplicate indexes should not replace it when maximizing length.

qa: Why not use sliding windows for every sum problem?

The window must have a monotone relationship between boundary changes and validity. Negative values can make extension reduce the sum or removal increase it, invalidating the simple positive-input argument.
Why is the initial zero prefix necessary?
It represents ranges that start at index zero. Without it, a prefix equal to the target has no earlier boundary in the map and is incorrectly omitted.
When do I store earliest versus latest indexes?

It depends on the objective. Earliest positions often maximize length; latest can minimize it under the appropriate contract. Counts are needed when all matching ranges contribute. Choose state from the requested result, not from a memorized template.
pitfalls: Applying a positive-sum window to arbitrary signed values.
Moving the left boundary backward after a repeated character.
Replacing frequency counts with a set and losing valid ranges.
readiness: Window validity and update order are explicit.
Counterexamples distinguish windows from prefix methods.
Zero and repeated-prefix cases are covered.
The stored map state matches the optimization or counting goal.

title: Trees and Graphs: Traverse with a Purpose
duration: 3 weeks of traversal and modeling practice
audience: Learners who know BFS and DFS names but need to choose traversal state, visitation timing, and graph modeling correctly for unfamiliar problems.
summary: A traversal is a framework for exploring a state space while preserving the information needed by the problem. Decide what a node and edge represent, whether the graph is directed or weighted, and whether you need reachability, shortest distance, ordering, or an aggregate over subtrees.
outcomes: Model graph state and choose adjacency representations from the workload.
Use BFS for equal-cost shortest paths and DFS for appropriate structural reasoning.
Handle cycles, disconnected components, and recursion depth deliberately.
Explain topological ordering and why weighted paths need additional assumptions.
foundations: Model before traversing

A node might be a cell, a word, a task, or a compound state such as position plus remaining budget. If future choices depend on information not in the node identity, the visited set can incorrectly merge different states.
Visited timing controls work

For ordinary BFS, marking on enqueue prevents duplicate queue entries and preserves a clean layer interpretation. DFS cycle detection on a directed graph needs active-path state, not just one global visited bit. Undirected traversal must account for the parent edge.
Traversal order carries meaning

BFS discovers minimum edge count in an unweighted graph. Postorder can compute child results before a parent. A topological order respects dependencies only when the directed graph is acyclic. Choose the order because the proof needs it.
studyRule: Draw a small graph and annotate the queue or stack at each step. Include a cycle and a disconnected component. Implement both recursive and iterative versions where useful, and account for call-stack depth rather than treating recursion as free memory.
plan: Week 1
Tree state

Practice preorder, inorder, postorder, level order, height, and path constraints. Define what each recursive call returns versus what is accumulated globally. Test empty and skewed trees and compare node identity with stored values.
A traversal trace and a subtree computation with a clear return-value invariant.
Week 2
Graph exploration

Implement adjacency lists, grid neighbors, components, BFS distances, and cycle detection. Decide when to mark visited and whether mutation of the input is allowed. Compare O(V+E) traversal with dense matrix costs.
Tests for cycles, duplicate edges where allowed, isolated nodes, and unreachable destinations.
Week 3, first half
Dependencies and weights

Study indegrees and topological sorting, then compare BFS with Dijkstra under nonnegative weights. Explain why negative edges violate Dijkstra's settled-distance argument and why a stop budget may belong in the state.
A dependency-order example and a shortest-path decision table tied to edge assumptions.
Week 3, second half
Unseen modeling
Solve a transformation, scheduling, or constrained-path problem without a visible graph label. State the node identity, transitions, objective, and visited contract before choosing a traversal.
A new problem modeled correctly and checked with a counterexample to an oversimplified state.

lab.title: Schedule tasks and detect a dependency cycle
lab.scenario: Tasks A and B must finish before C; C must finish before D. You need a valid execution order or a clear report that the dependency graph contains a cycle.
steps: Create edges A->C, B->C, and C->D, with indegrees zero, zero, two, and one. Enqueue every zero-indegree task, not just an arbitrary starting node, because the graph may have several independent sources.
Remove A and B in either order, decrementing C's indegree for each completed dependency. C becomes ready only after both decrements. Removing C then makes D ready. One valid result is A, B, C, D.

Add edge D->B. After processing A, the remaining B-C-D cycle never reaches zero indegree. If the number processed is less than the number of tasks, report a cycle rather than returning a misleading partial schedule.
lab.result: The indegree invariant counts unresolved prerequisites. The algorithm takes O(V+E) time with adjacency lists and detects that no complete topological order exists when a cycle remains.
checks: Are all initial zero-indegree nodes included?
Does every edge decrement its destination exactly once?
Is a partial result rejected when not all tasks were processed?
lab.extension: Add task durations and ask for the earliest completion time under unlimited workers. Propagate the maximum predecessor finish time along the topological order; do not confuse this with resource-limited scheduling.

qa: Why is BFS not always the right shortest-path algorithm?

It minimizes edge count when each edge has equal cost. Different nonnegative weights need an algorithm such as Dijkstra; negative weights require other reasoning. The graph's weight contract determines the choice.
Can I use one visited bit for every cycle problem?

No. Directed-cycle detection often needs unvisited, active, and finished states, or an indegree-based method. Seeing a previously finished node is not the same as finding a back edge to the active path.
What if recursive DFS overflows the stack?
Use an explicit stack or another traversal when depth can be large. State the input bound and memory model; a correct recursive idea still needs an implementation that handles the permitted depth.
pitfalls: Using an incomplete node identity for a constrained path problem.
Assuming a visited node always implies a directed cycle.
Ignoring disconnected components or recursion-depth limits.
readiness: Node, edge, and visited-state meanings are explicit.
Traversal order is justified by the objective.
Cycles and unreachable states are handled correctly.
Complexity is expressed in the relevant vertices, edges, or grid cells.

title: Dynamic Programming Without Guessing
audience: Candidates who can follow a DP solution after reading it but struggle to define the state, recurrence, base cases, and iteration order independently.
summary: Dynamic programming reuses solutions to repeated subproblems whose relevant history can be represented by a state. Start with the meaning of a state and the final answer, then derive transitions and boundaries. Memorizing a table shape without this meaning makes variants difficult to solve.
outcomes: Define a state that contains exactly the information future decisions need.
Derive transitions, base cases, and valid evaluation order from that state.
Distinguish counting, feasibility, minimum-cost, and maximum-value objectives.
Optimize memory only after explaining dependencies and preserving correctness.
foundations: State is a sufficient summary

If two histories produce the same state, their future options and objective contribution must be equivalent under the recurrence. Missing a remaining budget, last choice, or position can merge subproblems that actually differ. Too much history creates an unnecessarily large state space.
Base cases define semantics

An empty prefix, zero remaining amount, or completed target often has a special value. For counting, one empty construction can be correct; for minimization, unreachable states need a sentinel. A wrong base case can make a plausible recurrence consistently wrong.
Order enforces reuse rules

In-place updates can accidentally reuse an item more than once or count permutations instead of combinations. Determine whether a transition reads the previous layer or current layer before choosing loop order or compressing a table.
studyRule: For every problem, write four sentences before code: state meaning, transition, base cases, and answer location. Begin with memoized recursion when it clarifies the model, then derive bottom-up order and account for recursion depth.
plan: Week 1, first half
One-dimensional decisions

Practice stairs, non-adjacent selection, and minimum coin count. Draw the recursion tree and identify repeated states. Distinguish the value returned by a state from the decision path used to reconstruct a solution.
A recurrence with explicit unreachable and empty-input behavior, checked against brute force on small cases.
Week 1, second half
Counting and reuse

Compare subset sum, unbounded coin combinations, and ordered compositions. Trace updates for a tiny target and explain how loop direction controls reuse. Do not transfer a loop nest from one contract without proof.
A small example where two superficially similar loop orders intentionally produce different counts.
Week 2
Two-dimensional states

Study sequence alignment, edit distance, and grid paths. Define what each prefix index represents and which earlier states a cell depends on. Initialize empty rows and columns according to the actual operations.
A filled small table whose every transition can be explained in words.
Week 3
Optimize and generalize

Practice interval or constrained states relevant to your level. Estimate state count times transition cost. Compress memory only after proving overwritten values are no longer needed, then run unseen mixed variants.
A complete solution with a correctness argument, complexity, and tests that detect update-order mistakes.

lab.title: Count combinations, not orderings
lab.scenario: With unlimited positive coin values 1 and 2, count ways to make amount 3 when order does not matter. The valid combinations are 1+1+1 and 1+2, so the answer is two rather than three.
steps: Define ways[amount] as the number of combinations using coin types processed so far. Initialize ways[0] to one for the empty construction, and all positive amounts to zero.
Process coin 1 across amounts in increasing order, giving one way for every amount through 3. Then process coin 2: ways[2] gains ways[0], and ways[3] gains ways[1]. The final ways[3] is two.

Explain the alternative loop order: iterating target amounts outside and choosing the last coin inside counts ordered sequences, so 1+2 and 2+1 become different. Neither order is universally correct; the requested meaning decides.
lab.result: The recurrence and loop order now follow a precise counting contract. For c coin types and target A, this version takes O(c*A) time and O(A) auxiliary space, with positive coin values assumed.
checks: Does amount zero produce one empty combination?
Are repeated coin denominations normalized or otherwise handled according to the input contract?
Does the tiny amount-three example distinguish combinations from sequences?
lab.extension: Change the problem so each coin instance can be used only once. Explain why a backward amount traversal prevents reading a value updated by the same item during the current iteration.

qa: How do I recognize a DP problem?

Look for choices leading to repeated subproblems whose future depends on a compact state. Recursion alone is not enough: backtracking with mostly unique states may not benefit from memoization, and a greedy proof may eliminate the need for DP.
What is the complexity of memoization?

Count reachable states and the work per state, including loops, copying, and lookup costs. Also account for stored results and recursion depth. Saying O(n) because each function is cached can ignore many transitions.
Should I always compress to one row?

No. First obtain a correct state model and dependency order. A clear full table can be preferable during reasoning, especially if reconstruction is required. Compression is useful only when it preserves the needed previous values.
pitfalls: Writing a recurrence without defining what a cell means.
Using zero for both unreachable and valid zero-cost states.
Changing loop order without checking item reuse or counting semantics.
readiness: State, transition, boundaries, and answer location are explicit.
Small cases agree with an independent brute-force method.
Complexity counts both states and transitions.
Memory optimization has a dependency argument.

title: Heaps, Intervals, and Greedy Proofs
audience: Candidates who can use a priority queue but want to know when it is the right structure and how to justify a greedy choice instead of trusting that it seems locally best.
summary: Heaps maintain an extreme under updates, interval problems depend on endpoint semantics, and greedy algorithms need a proof that a local choice preserves an optimal solution. These tools often combine in scheduling and streaming problems, but each solves a different part of the reasoning.
outcomes: Maintain top-k or next-event state without sorting all data repeatedly.
Define interval overlap and tie handling before implementation.
Use exchange or dominance arguments to justify greedy decisions.
Recognize when weights or extra constraints require DP or another method.
foundations: A heap exposes one useful extreme

A min-heap gives the smallest element efficiently, but does not keep every element in sorted order for arbitrary queries. Top-k streaming commonly uses a size-k min-heap so its root is the weakest retained candidate. State what every heap entry means.
Endpoints are part of the contract

Half-open intervals [start,end) allow a meeting ending at time t to share a room with one starting at t. Closed intervals may have different overlap rules. Equal start/end times and zero-length intervals need an explicit interpretation.
Greedy requires exchangeability

For maximum count of non-overlapping intervals, choosing the earliest finishing compatible interval leaves at least as much room as another first choice. Weighted profit changes the objective and can invalidate this argument, even though the input still consists of intervals.
studyRule: Write a tiny counterexample to a tempting incorrect rule, such as choosing the shortest or highest-profit interval. Then state the proof for the chosen rule. Separate the algorithmic choice from the heap implementation that makes it efficient.
plan: Sessions 1-3
Priority queue operations
Practice insertion, extraction, bounded top-k, and merging sorted streams. Decide min-heap versus max-heap and include stable tie-breakers when values alone do not uniquely order entries.
A trace showing the invariant after every update and O(log k) versus O(log n) costs.
Sessions 4-6
Interval contracts

Solve merging, overlap detection, room allocation, and removal-count variants. Sort on the field needed by the proof, not automatically by start. Test touching endpoints and multiple simultaneous events.
A small suite that distinguishes half-open and closed interval behavior.
Sessions 7-10
Greedy correctness
Study earliest-finish scheduling, reachable-range expansion, and monotone choices. Explain an exchange or dominance argument. Compare with a weighted variant where the greedy rule fails.
One proof and one valid counterexample, both expressed in the problem's exact objective.
Sessions 11-14
Streaming and mixed practice
Combine heaps with offline sorting, query processing, or multiple streams. Remove expired or stale heap entries as required. Run a mixed problem without a topic hint and justify the retained state.
A tested solution that separates event eligibility, priority, and expiration clearly.

lab.title: Allocate the minimum number of meeting rooms
lab.scenario: Meetings use half-open time intervals. For [0,30), [5,10), and [15,20), determine the peak rooms required and explain why the first meeting can overlap both shorter meetings without requiring three rooms.
steps: Sort by start time and keep a min-heap of end times for active meetings. Before admitting a new meeting, remove every end time less than or equal to its start, because touching endpoints do not overlap under this contract.
At time 0, push 30. At time 5, no room is free, so push 10 and record a peak of two. At time 15, remove 10, retain 30, and push 20; the active count remains two.
Track the maximum heap size over the sweep. Explain that the heap models currently active meetings, not every meeting ever seen, and that removing expired entries is essential to this interpretation.
lab.result: The minimum room count is two: overlapping meetings require separate rooms, and the sweep reuses every available room. Sorting plus heap updates takes O(n log n) time and O(n) worst-case auxiliary space.
checks: Do [0,5) and [5,10) reuse one room?
Are all ended meetings removed before counting active demand?
Does the result reflect the peak rather than only the final heap size?
lab.extension: Change the goal to selecting a maximum-profit compatible subset. Show a case where earliest finish loses to a more valuable interval, then formulate a weighted scheduling DP instead of reusing the room-count algorithm.

qa: Is the heap array sorted?

No. It satisfies a parent-child priority invariant sufficient to expose the root. Iterating its storage does not generally produce sorted order. Use extraction or sorting when ordered enumeration is required.
Why keep a min-heap for the largest k values?

The smallest retained value is the replacement threshold. A new value no larger than it cannot improve the retained set; a larger value replaces it. This bounds memory to k rather than storing the entire stream.
How do I know a greedy choice is valid?

Provide an exchange, dominance, or invariant argument showing it can be part of an optimum. Test variants and counterexamples. Local attractiveness is not a proof, especially when weights or dependencies change the objective.
pitfalls: Confusing heap order with fully sorted order.
Leaving interval endpoint semantics unspecified.
Applying an unweighted greedy rule to weighted optimization.
readiness: Heap entries and their priority have explicit meanings.
Overlap rules and ties are tested.
Greedy choices have a correctness argument.
A changed objective triggers a fresh analysis.

title: Binary Search, Sorting, and Boundary Proofs
audience: Candidates who repeatedly encounter off-by-one errors or use binary search by template without explaining why a candidate region can be discarded.
summary: Binary search finds a boundary in an ordered or monotone search space. Its correctness depends on the meaning of the bounds and the update rule. Sorting creates useful order but has its own cost, stability, and memory implications. Learn both as reasoning tools rather than syntax patterns.
outcomes: Implement lower and upper bounds with a consistent interval convention.
Recognize monotone feasibility and search over answers safely.
Explain sorting cost, stability, and the effect on original positions.
Prove termination and test minimal and boundary cases.
foundations: Define the boundary

A lower bound is the first position whose value is at least the target; an upper bound is the first position greater than it. These remain useful even when the target is absent. Decide whether the interval is closed or half-open and keep all updates consistent.
Monotone predicates extend the method

Capacity or speed problems can have a false-then-true feasibility predicate. Search for the first feasible answer only after proving the monotonicity and establishing valid bounds. The cost includes every feasibility check, not just the logarithmic number of iterations.
Sorting changes the problem state

Sorting can enable pointer sweeps and grouping, but may mutate input or lose original order. Stable sorting preserves equal-key order, which matters for some contracts. Library time and auxiliary-memory guarantees vary, so cite the actual implementation model.
studyRule: Use one clear lower-bound implementation until its invariant is natural. Draw the retained interval after each comparison. For answer search, test the feasibility function independently before combining it with binary search.
plan: Sessions 1-3
Bound conventions

Implement exact search and lower bound with half-open intervals. Test empty input, one element, target below all values, target above all values, and duplicates. Explain what positions are known impossible after each update.
A trace proving the interval shrinks and the final position satisfies the boundary definition.
Sessions 4-5
Duplicates and derived queries
Use lower and upper bounds to find a target range or count occurrences. Preserve original indexes if sorting is introduced. Avoid special-case logic that contradicts the chosen interval convention.
Tests showing absent targets and repeated values produce correct ranges and counts.
Sessions 6-8
Search on an answer

Practice minimum capacity or speed with a monotone feasibility check. Derive low and high bounds from the input, use integer arithmetic for ceilings, and state whether the answer is guaranteed to exist.
A separately tested predicate and a complexity formula including its linear or other cost.
Sessions 9-10
Sorting trade-offs and mixed problems

Compare sorting with hashing and selection. Discuss stable order, comparator consistency, worst-case versus expected bounds, and output requirements. Solve an unseen problem that does not explicitly mention binary search.
A justified choice of ordering or monotonicity rather than a memorized problem label.

lab.title: Find the first value at least a target
lab.scenario: For sorted values [1,3,3,7] and target 3, the answer is index 1. For target 4, it is index 3. A boundary search should handle both without assuming the target exists.
steps: Maintain a half-open candidate interval [left,right), initially [0,4). Values before left are known smaller than the target, and the answer can be right as an insertion position. Compute a midpoint inside the interval.

If the midpoint value is smaller than the target, move left to midpoint plus one. Otherwise move right to midpoint, retaining it as a possible first qualifying position. For target 3, equal values move the right boundary leftward.

Stop when left equals right. Verify the position is either the array length or a qualifying value, and that the preceding value, if any, is smaller. This postcondition is stronger than merely checking a few returned indexes.
lab.result: The same O(log n)-time, O(1)-auxiliary-space boundary method supports insertion positions and duplicate ranges. Its correctness follows from retained candidates and a shrinking interval.
checks: Does an empty array return insertion position zero?
Do targets below and above all values return zero and length?
Do duplicates return the first qualifying index rather than an arbitrary match?
lab.extension: Replace array lookup with a shipping-capacity feasibility function. Prove that increasing capacity cannot require more days, then explain why total complexity is O(n log R) for answer range R rather than simply O(log n).

qa: Why does binary search sometimes loop forever?

An update may leave the interval unchanged, often because midpoint is retained on the wrong side under a mismatched convention. State the bounds precisely and prove each branch strictly reduces the candidate range.
Can I binary-search any boolean function?

No. The relevant truth values must have a monotone boundary over the searched domain, and the interval must bracket the answer appropriately. Without that property, discarding half the domain can remove valid answers.
Is sorting always O(n log n) and in-place?

Not universally. Algorithms and language libraries have different worst-case, expected, stability, and auxiliary-memory properties. Analyze the chosen implementation and include copies or index-pair storage required by the problem.
pitfalls: Mixing closed and half-open bound updates.
Using floating-point arithmetic where integer feasibility is required.
Ignoring the cost of a feasibility check or input copy.
readiness: The search invariant and termination argument are explicit.
Boundary and duplicate cases pass.
Monotonicity is proved before searching an answer space.
Sorting and memory costs match the actual implementation.

title: Explain Correctness, Complexity, and Tests
duration: 2 weeks, then use in every coding session
audience: Candidates who often reach a plausible implementation but struggle to justify it, test systematically, or give complexity that matches the actual code.
summary: A complete coding answer includes a contract, a reason the algorithm is correct, an implementation, tests, and a realistic cost analysis. These are not optional finishing touches. They expose assumptions early and help you recover from feedback without replacing the whole solution blindly.
outcomes: Turn an ambiguous prompt into explicit input and output assumptions.
Use invariants, induction, or exchange reasoning at an appropriate level.
Design tests from failure modes rather than random happy-path examples.
Include library operations, copies, recursion, and output size in complexity.
foundations: Clarification is part of solving

Ask about duplicates, sortedness, mutation, missing answers, size limits, and return format when relevant. Do not ask every possible question mechanically; resolve the assumptions that change the algorithm or its safety.
An invariant connects iterations

State what is true before and after each step, why initialization establishes it, why the update preserves it, and why termination yields the answer. Recursive solutions use an analogous subproblem contract. The explanation should match the code, not a different ideal algorithm.
Tests discriminate hypotheses

A useful test targets a boundary, duplicate, stale state, overflow, or invalid assumption. Tiny counterexamples are easier to trace. Compare with an independent brute-force oracle on small random inputs when the problem permits it.
studyRule: Reserve a fixed portion of each practice session for explanation and tests. After coding, read the implementation as if reviewing someone else's work: identify hidden copies, stale variables, mutation, and failure paths before reporting a complexity class.
plan: Days 1-3
Contract and baseline
Rewrite several prompts as concise contracts. Implement or describe a simple correct baseline and identify its repeated work. State which constraints justify an optimization.
A contract and baseline for each problem, including no-answer and minimal-input behavior.
Days 4-6
Correctness arguments

Practice one loop invariant, one recursive induction, and one greedy exchange argument. Align variables in the explanation with the implementation. Ask a peer to find an update that might break the invariant.
A short proof sketch that survives a changed example and does not merely restate the code.
Days 7-10
Adversarial tests

Build tests for empty/minimal input where allowed, duplicates, ties, monotone extremes, and absent answers. Use exhaustive or randomized small cases against a baseline to catch overlooked combinations.
At least one regression case that fails the buggy version and passes the corrected one.
Days 11-14
Cost and communication

Audit loops, recursion depth, sorting, substring creation, hash operations, and output size. Run a timed mock with an explicit testing segment. Explain a bug correction through the broken invariant rather than apologizing vaguely.
A complete solution narrative with justified costs and a reproducible set of checks.

lab.title: Use a brute-force oracle to test an optimized method
lab.scenario: You optimize a contiguous-range calculation from quadratic time to a linear scan. The examples pass, but an update-order bug may remain. Small inputs make exhaustive comparison practical.
steps: Write a straightforward baseline that enumerates every valid range and computes the requested result directly. Keep it structurally different from the optimized code so both are less likely to share the same mistake.

Generate short arrays from a small value set, including zero, duplicates, and negative values when allowed. Compare outputs for each array and target. Stop at the first mismatch and shrink it to the smallest explanatory input.

Trace the optimized state on that input, identify the violated invariant, and add a fixed regression case before correcting the implementation. Rerun the same exhaustive comparison and neighboring boundaries afterward.
lab.result: The oracle supplies evidence against implementation defects while the invariant explains general correctness. Exhaustive small tests do not prove every large input, but they are highly effective at finding boundary and state-update errors.
checks: Does the baseline implement the same output contract?
Are generated inputs restricted to the allowed domain?
Is the baseline independent enough to avoid reproducing the optimized bug?
lab.extension: Add a performance comparison only after outputs agree. Use increasing sizes and record the workload; do not infer asymptotic behavior from one tiny example or ignore the cost of generating the input.

qa: Can tests replace a correctness proof?

No finite ordinary test set covers every possible input, but tests are essential for validating implementation and assumptions. A practical interview answer combines a concise proof argument with targeted tests rather than choosing one or the other.
Should output memory count as space?

State the convention. Report auxiliary working memory separately from output when useful, but do not hide a large output or copied input. Recursion stacks and library-created temporary objects are also real space costs.
What should I say when a test reveals a bug?

Explain the failing case, identify the broken invariant, make the smallest grounded correction, and rerun the case plus related boundaries. This demonstrates precise debugging and is better than defending the incorrect result.
pitfalls: Reporting complexity for an idea rather than the actual implementation.
Testing only the examples supplied in the prompt.
Using a baseline that shares the same optimization and bug.
readiness: Input and output assumptions are explicit.
The correctness argument matches the implementation.
Tests target meaningful failure modes and boundaries.
Complexity includes copies, recursion, and output conventions.
